ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows an equilateral triangle and a circle concentrically superimposed. The outer contour is neither a complete triangle nor a complete circle, but is composed of straight side segments near the three vertices of the triangle, and three circular arcs of the circle protruding outward from the middle parts of the three sides of the triangle; the part of the circle inside the triangle is represented with dashed lines. Reasoning: The problem gives that the side length of the equilateral triangle is 3, the radius of the circle is 1, and the two have the same center. The radius of the incircle of the equilateral triangle, that is, the distance from the center to each side, is 3√3/6 = √3/2. The circle intersects each side of the triangle, and the chord length cut out is 2√(1 - (√3/2)^2) = 2√(1/4) = 1. Therefore the middle length 1 of each side of the triangle is covered by the circle and does not belong to the outer perimeter; the straight boundary length left on each side is 3 - 1 = 2. The three sides contribute a total of 3 × 2 = 6. The central angle corresponding to this chord is 2 arccos(√3/2) = π/3, so the length of each exposed circular arc is 1 × π/3 = π/3. There are three such circular arcs, and the total arc length is π. Thus the total perimeter is 6 + π.
